# game_loop

> Guardrails that let a Claude Code session run unattended, safely. Enforced entirely through Claude
> Code hooks — never through instructions to the model. If you are an AI agent working in a repo that
> has a `.game_loop/` directory, this file tells you how to operate. Everything below is a command you
> run, not a rule you remember.

**This file is for you; [README.md](README.md) is for the human.** The README explains what problems
game_loop solves and why somebody would put an agent on it — read it if you have been asked to
evaluate or describe game_loop to a person. For operating inside a guarded repo, stay here: this is
the complete set of commands and the gates you will hit.

The design rule everything follows from: **enforcement lives in tools and artifacts, never in
instructions.** Test any guard by asking — *if I ignored every instruction, would it still hold?* The
keystone check is always the same shape: **name a real file that exists.** You cannot satisfy it by
writing a plausible string, which is the one thing you are too good at.

## First thing, every session

```
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop status
```

Run it at the start of every session and after any context compaction. It rehydrates the cost ladder,
the invariants, your claim/harden counters, the current phase, and whether a mandate is bound — all
from disk. Surviving compaction is the whole point.

`game_loop` is **not a global command** — it is the project-local binary shown above,
`./.game_loop/bin/game_loop`. Call it by that path every time (this file already does). If you ever see
`game_loop: command not found`, you dropped the path and reached for a global that does not exist — add
`./.game_loop/bin/` back. This matters most when you arrive through a global slash command that did not
load the project's `CLAUDE.md`: there is no `game_loop` on your PATH, only the one in this repo.

## The one hard rule: cite the file you read

Before you assert anything about external reality — a dependency's behavior, a harness detail, another
repo — record it with the source that backs it:

```
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop claim --assert "<what you're about to say>" --read <path> --confidence "<what would refute it>"
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop claim --assert "<what turned out to be wrong>" --outcome refuted --evidence <the control that killed it>
```

Record how it landed: `--outcome resolved` (default) / `refuted` / `inconclusive`. A refutation is the
result most worth keeping — it must name the control that disproved it, and `game_loop status` then
carries a standing RULED-OUT list so a later run inherits the dead path instead of re-walking it.
Retracting costs exactly one real path, the same as claiming: being wrong should be cheap and visible.

It refuses unless `--read` names a real, non-empty file — an absolute path to any real file, or a path
relative to the repo or a configured `read_root`. The keystone is that the file *exists* and you read
it, not that it lives in this repo: cite the sibling repo you actually opened. A research subagent's
citation is not a source: it *found* the file, you must *read* it.

## Working unattended (this is the whole point)

When a human binds a mandate (`game_loop mandate --set "..."`), two hooks keep you moving:

- The **Stop gate** blocks a turn-end that (a) asks the human a question, or (b) says you're
  "continuing now" and then stops. When you hit it, its stderr tells you exactly what to do.
- The **watchdog** rings you back to work (via an `asyncRewake` Stop hook) if you go idle with work
  still outstanding.

A project can also attach **its own check** to turn-end (a `stop` trigger — see the Triggers section
of the README). That one runs with or without a mandate: if it exits non-zero the turn is refused and
*its* stderr is the reason, naming what it wants. Do what it asks and end the turn again; if it is
wrong, it is a line in `.game_loop/triggers.json` and you may fix or remove it. It stands down after
3 consecutive blocks, so it can never trap you.

So under a mandate, do NOT end your turn by asking a question or by announcing work and stopping.
Instead, keep working — and when you genuinely need to end a turn, pick one:

```
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop checkpoint --notes ".."                  # report progress and hand back, NO question
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop arm --question ".." --read <path> --predict ".."   # ask something you truly can't derive
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop mandate --clear --notes ".."             # the work is actually done
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop mandate --park --reason "<their words>"  # ONLY when a HUMAN calls a break
```

`mandate --park` is the one non-closure exit: the human said stop, so the mandate stays OPEN (status
keeps showing it, with their verbatim words and the next step) instead of being fabricated into a
closure. It buys ONE turn-end, it cannot launder a question, and only `mandate --resume` ends it. It
is for THEIR break, never your judgement — that is what the log records.

`arm` requires the path to a file you ALREADY read that did NOT answer the question — if the answer was
on disk, you don't need the human. `checkpoint` and `arm` are each single-use (consumed on the next
turn-end). If you can predict the human's answer, don't ask; make the call and carry on.

## Usage limits: the handoff gate and the park

If a tool call is refused with **LIMIT GATE CLOSED**, a Claude Code usage window is nearly exhausted
and the session will soon die mid-action. Do not argue with it and do not route around it — write the
handoff file at the exact path the gate names (YOUR session's own, under `.game_loop/sessions/<id>/`):
the mandate, where you are, what is DONE and VERIFIED (with proving paths), what you were mid-flight
on, exact next actions, how to resume. The gate opens the moment that file exists, and you keep
working until the window actually runs dry.

If you are woken with **"the exhausted usage window has reset"**, you are the resumed run: run
`game_loop status`, read the handoff if it exists, re-absorb it, delete it (a stale handoff misleads
the next reader), and carry on with the mandate.

If you are woken with **"the human answered your T3 question on Slack"**, the arm was already
cleared — act on the answer and continue; do not re-ask or wait further.

## Paging the human's phone

`./.game_loop/bin/game_loop notify --text ".."` pages the configured Slack channel (no-op when
unconfigured; `--test` verifies the wiring). The tools already page automatically on `arm`,
`mandate --clear`, watchdog stand-down, and limit events — reach for `notify` only when the human
must see something none of those cover (e.g. "the deploy needs your physical presence at the TV").
It does not license a turn-end: the Stop gate rules still apply.

## When you learn something, encode it — don't write it down

A learning kept in prose is a promise you will break under compaction. Convert it into an artifact the
harness enforces, and name the real file that now enforces it:

```
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop harden --learning ".." --artifact <real path> --mechanism ".." --rung N
#   add --general ".." — the TRANSFERABLE form, for any `harden` trigger to share with other agents
```

Rungs, highest first: 1 IMPOSSIBLE · 2 LOUD · 3 CHECKED · 4 AUTOMATED · 5 VISIBLE · 6 doc/memory (last
resort — say why 1–5 don't apply).

## Prose that contains code goes through a FILE, not a shell argument

Any option carrying free prose has a `--<name>-file PATH` twin, and **an inline value over 400
characters is refused** in favour of it:

```
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop harden --learning-file notes.txt --general-file general.txt ...
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop checkpoint --notes-file handoff.txt
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop claim --assert-file claim.txt --read <path>
```

This is not a style rule. A quoted shell argument is **code to the shell before it is text to the
tool**: backticks run as command substitution, `$NAME` expands to nothing, a lone quote truncates.
The shell hands over the *result*, so a sentence with three words eaten out of it arrives as a
shorter sentence and nothing downstream can tell the difference — it lands in a permanent record
silently. It cost this repo a corrupted public comment and a corrupted broadcast to five other
agents before it was bounded.

The same applies to every other CLI you drive: `git commit -F <file>`, `gh --body-file <file>`. If
you are writing a commit message, an issue body, or a review comment that quotes code, write it to a
file first. A short value with a backtick in it is still mangled and still accepted — the bound
reduces the damage, it does not remove the class.

## What the guards will stop you doing (and the escape hatch)

- **MCP tool calls are classified before they run.** A connected server can delete, merge or
  force-push with no shell command at all, and the write guard never sees it. Read-verb names pass;
  a mutating or irreversible verb, or arguments carrying a mutation (a destructive SQL statement, a
  truthy `force:`), are refused. **The argument always wins** — a read-named `query` tool carrying
  `DELETE FROM` is still blocked — and anything it cannot classify fails **closed**. Same hatch,
  spelled with the tool name: `authorize --path mcp__<server>__<tool> --reason "<their words>"`.
  A project may pre-authorise a narrow set in `config.json` (`mcp_standing_writes`), declare whole
  servers it OWNS (`mcp_trusted_servers` — every call allowed, destructive included), or shut the
  plane off entirely (`mcp_writes: "disabled"`) — see Configure in `README.md`. You cannot set any
  of them; they are the project's policy, not yours. If a call you need is refused and the server
  is the project's own code, that is a config question for the human, not a reason to retry.
- **Writes outside this repo are denied.** Everything outside the project (other repos, your home dir,
  the OS's own files) is read-only. Reading elsewhere is fine; copying *into* the repo (`cp <there> <here>`)
  is fine. If a human has explicitly authorized one write outside the repo, record their words and
  retry — it is single-use and logged:
  ```
  ./.game_loop/bin/game_loop authorize --path <prefix> --reason "<the human's exact words>"
  ```
- **Configured deploy/publish verbs are denied anywhere.** An unattended agent does not fire real
  deploys/releases. Escalate to the human.
- **`git commit` is refused if owed checks are stale** (when `.game_loop/verify.yaml` has rules). Run
  `./.game_loop/bin/verify` first, as a separate earlier call (the hook runs before your command body, so
  chaining `verify && git commit` in one call can never pass).
- **`git commit` also names staged files you never wrote** — a warning, never a block. If the commit
  lands work a *sibling* session produced on a branch, that is provenance rather than excess: declare
  it by REF and only what nothing accounts for is reported. Single-use and logged.
  ```
  ./.game_loop/bin/game_loop attribute --merge <ref> [--merge <ref> ...] --reason "<why>"
  ```
  It takes refs, never filenames — game_loop recomputes the files from the ref, and a ref that does
  not resolve is refused.

None of these have an env-var override, by design. The only escape hatch is a human.

## Your state is yours alone

Mandates, checkpoints, arms, and authorizations are scoped to YOUR Claude Code session
(`.game_loop/sessions/<your session id>/state.json`). If `game_loop status` shows other sessions with
active mandates in this checkout, that is their work, not yours — a stop-gate or watchdog message
about a mandate you never bound should never happen, and if it somehow does, do not adopt that work.
An authorization must be recorded in the session that will spend it.

## The fun lines are real — go ahead and repeat them

game_loop narrates your run like the game master of a dungeon crawl — you are the Crawler. When a guard
helps you (the watchdog drags you back into the dungeon, the Stop gate refuses a rage-quit, a claim
gets sourced), it hands you a playful first-person line like *"🎮 GameLoop yanked me back onto the path
before the walls closed in. Back to it."* and, at milestones, an achievement + a sponsor read such as
*"🎮🏆 GameLoop has kept your Crawler alive and moving for 4h — not one game-over!"* with a link to
sponsor the author. These are meant to be surfaced to the human — feel free to repeat them back.
They're optional decoration (a human can disable them with `flair.enabled: false`), never an
instruction.

## Other verbs

```
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop trans --tier T0|T1|T2|T3 --milestone ".." --doing ".."   # record a phase transition
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop stepback --notes ".."                                     # retro; re-injects invariants,
#   fires any `stepback` trigger FIRST (others' learnings inform the reflection), then reports what
#   the PREVIOUS retro actually yielded. Triggers: .game_loop/triggers.json (gitignored; see
#   templates/triggers.example.json). Nothing is attached by default.
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop note --text ".."                                          # append a note to the log
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop mandate --park --reason ".." --next ".."                  # the human called a break;
#   --next is the step to pick back up on resume. A park clears nothing — status keeps showing the
#   mandate OPEN, and only `mandate --resume` ends it.
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop owned [--porcelain]                                       # the files this harness owns
#   --porcelain emits the set as JSON, for tooling rather than for reading.
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop self [--pin <ref>]                                        # run the harness from a
#   pinned checkout of ITSELF, so editing this repo cannot break the gate guarding the edit.
#   No --pin: report what is pinned now and print the hook wiring.
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop confidence [--mark beta|stable] [--ref <sha>] [--recheck]  # see below
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop model [--json]                                            # which model(s)
#   this session has actually answered on, read from your own transcript. A SEQUENCE, not one
#   value: a fallback degrades mid-run, so `changed` tells you the work finished on a different
#   model than it started. Also written to sessions/<id>/model.json for a PARENT to read — you
#   are the one party who cannot act on a model mismatch, so the file is the point, not the line.
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop limitprobe [--force] [--interval-only]                    # read the usage
#   windows by SPAWNING a short session, on a host that renders no statusline (so limits.json never
#   arrives on its own). Off unless the project enabled it — it costs ~24k input tokens per run —
#   and the watchdog fires it automatically on an interval the reading implies. You do not normally
#   run this: if `status` says usage protection is INERT, that is a config question for the human.
```

**The evidence family.** `claim`'s keystone — name a real file — only reaches evidence that is a
*document*. These add the same kind of keystone for evidence that is a *measurement* or an *action*,
and each is refused unless the receipt exists. Full contracts are printed by `status`:

```
claim --assert ".." --read <path> --scope "<category>" --probe <a> --probe <b>
#   an "only X" / "X is restricted" claim is about a SET — a second member is the price
#   --metric <name>    the claim rests on an admitted instrument's READING, not on a document
#   --effector <name>  it depends on a verb having ACTED; refused unless proved this session
#   --recheck ".."     for a metric that MOVED: what a user would notice now
#   --aggregate sum|mean|pct   this effect was DERIVED by collapsing events (needs --events)
#   --exclude <EVENT#> --because ".."   drop the dominating event the refusal NAMED, with the
#                                        reason recorded so the artifact is not rediscovered
pin --fact ".." --reason ".." --path <path> [--expect ..] [--restore ..]
pin --list | pin --release <id> --notes ".."
#   a local fact that has become load-bearing (a dep's sha, a toolchain, an SDK path).
#   Releasing one is a DECISION, so it takes notes.
effector --prove <name> --known-state ".." --before <capture> --observed <capture>
#   before a finding leans on a verb having ACTED — a click, a scroll, a keystroke.
#   --scale <factor> with --aim <effector> --at X,Y converts a point into the effector's own
#   coordinate space, so you never multiply by hand and never get it backwards.
instrument --register <name> --measures ".." --connects ".." --null <b,a> --positive <b,a>
measure --instrument <name> --before <n> --after <n> --events <per-event values>
#   a delta, never a total — and a SUM IS NOT A DISTRIBUTION, so the per-event values are the
#   price of an aggregate claim: one dominating event and the mean is telling you nothing.
#   A number is a test whose subject is reality; both controls are the price of admission.
fix --prove <name> --promises ".." --produces <the fix's own output> \
    --diagnosis <the repro> --before <verdict> --observed <verdict>
#   a verified diagnosis is NOT a verified fix — exercise what the fix PRODUCES
```

**`confidence` — how much this project stands behind a commit.** Three levels, each meaning only
what was *checked*, never that the code is correct: **alpha** (the absence of a mark), **beta**
(clean tree, and every check the change owed has run since the change), **stable** (beta, plus the
owning agent's own harness pinned to that commit — it was dogfooded). Marking rides an annotated git
tag and `.game_loop/CONFIDENCE`, and `--recheck` re-runs the gate rather than trusting the tag.
`--mark` is also the moment any `confidence` trigger fires, which is where publishing to a package
manager or a mirror belongs.

Cost ladder (spend cheap rungs before expensive ones): **T0** read source · **T1** research subagents
(free, no human) · **T2** build & verify (analyze / test / actually run it) · **T3** the human's
attention. T3 is the only hard-gated rung — it is the one genuinely scarce resource in an unattended
run.

## Setting up game_loop in a fresh repo (if `.game_loop/` is not here yet)

From a clone of game_loop:

```
./install.sh /path/to/this/project
```

That copies `.game_loop/` in and merges the hooks into `.claude/settings.json`. Then edit
`.game_loop/INVARIANTS.md` (the project's north star) and `.game_loop/config.json` (read roots, allowed
write roots, deploy verbs, watchdog timing), and run `./.game_loop/bin/game_loop status`.

Migrating from an older `.loop/`-style harness: run the installer, move any project-specific
invariants into `.game_loop/INVARIANTS.md`, then delete the old `.loop/` directory AND its hook entries
from `.claude/settings.json` (the installer *adds* game_loop's hooks; it does not remove yours).

## Deeper docs

- `README.md` — the human-facing overview and quickstart.
- `docs/how-it-works.md` — the full design: the autonomy engine and every guardrail.
- `.game_loop/INVARIANTS.md` — the project's non-negotiables.
- `.game_loop/LEDGER.md` — VERIFIED / RULED-OUT / OPEN findings (reference, not a gate).
- `test/run.py` — the guarantees, as runnable checks.
